$comment: Release budgets (cli-benchmarks / Y8). A ratchet that moves per PR is a record of what happened, not a limit on it — `benchmarks/axes/weight.ts` says so above RATIO_CEILING after four raises in one session. A budget lives here instead: set once for a release, from the measured distribution rather than from the last commit, and `scripts/release-budget-lock.test.ts` refuses to let a number here move unless `release` moves with it in the same commit.

bundled-bytes-ratio:burgee\u00f7cac.why: burgee's core bundle over cac's, the lightest zero-dependency incumbent in the field. cac has no --schema, no MCP surface and no manifest, so the denominator is a smaller package rather than a lighter one doing the same work; the ratio is published because a suite that only showed the five entry points we win is lying by selection. Raised 3.7 -> 3.9 on 2026-09-15 for PLAN 3.2's cosmiconfig surface. Lowered 3.9 -> 2.8 for wave-4 on 2026-09-21: measured 2.740 after the root barrel stopped re-exporting five optional modules (D-101), under the metric that counts the whole startup graph rather than the entry chunk (D-100). A ceiling left at 3.9 would be headroom nobody decided to grant. D-102 records that <= 1 is not reachable by engineering: cac is 10,457 bundled bytes of parser and help renderer, and the measured floor for an engine that also coerces values, resolves configuration, binds shutdown and detects an agent is near 2.26x.

derivedFrom.rule: mean + 3 sd = 38,987 bytes, which is 3.73x cac's 10,452. Rounded down to 3.7: three sigma is where the band itself calls a single point an act-now breach, so a budget above it would admit growth the watcher already refuses.
derivedFrom.note: This band breached at 1 sigma on 2026-09-10 — Rule 4, eight consecutive above the mean. The budget is set from the distribution anyway, and deliberately: a budget derived from a drifting series still bounds the drift, and lowering it is the next release's decision to take with the trend in hand.

deviation.why: Not derived from the distribution below, and deliberately so: the distribution is of a different quantity. Those 41 observations were taken under `--outfile`, which inlines every literal-specifier `await import()` into one file; the metric now counts the entry chunk plus the transitive closure of its `import` statements (D-100), and there is exactly ONE observation of the new tree under the new metric. A mean and a standard deviation cannot be computed from one point, so 2.8 is what this file's own $comment warns about — a ceiling set just above a single measurement (2.740) rather than above a spread — and it is written down as that rather than dressed as derived. It is set low rather than left high because the alternative is 1.16 of unearned headroom on a number this release halved. The next release re-derives it from `core-bundled-bytes` once the band holds observations under the new metric; until then, a breach here means look at the series, not at the code.

bundled-bytes-ratio:burgee\u00f7cac.note: Was BREACHED at 5.348 through the composition wave; it is not now. Measured 2.740 on 2026-09-21 with the core at 28,637 bundled bytes against cac's 10,457, which is the lowest this ratio has ever read. One sentence of the old note is retracted: it said lazy-loading help "measures +767 bytes rather than fewer, because esbuild inlines a literal-specifier dynamic import and then charges for the wrapper". That was true of the instrument, not of the code — `--outfile` has no chunks, so it inlined every dynamic import and charged the wrapper on top. Under `--splitting --outdir` the same laziness is worth what it always was, and the barrel split it enabled took the core from 57,880 to 28,637. The general lesson is the one this repository keeps relearning: a measurement that cannot see the thing you are optimising will tell you the optimisation does not work.
